set.longDescription:
Tamriel Rebuilt is one of modding's longest-running projects: a volunteer effort, more than two decades old, to build the rest of the Morrowind mainland that Bethesda's game only hints at from Vvardenfell's shores. Roughly half of that province is now finished, and it is released in expansions that sit beside the original game rather than replacing it.

The scale is hard to overstate. Grasping Fortune alone brought Narsis, the capital of House Hlaalu, with over 270 quests, 140 dungeons and more than 2,500 characters. Andaram added new biomes and nine faction questlines, while the newest release, Poison Song, combines more new content with a revamp of older areas. All of it is written and built to feel as if it could have shipped with Morrowind itself, with the same dense books and the same indifference to whether you are ready.

It requires both Tribunal and Bloodmoon, and it keeps its art in a separate Tamriel_Data package. This edition handles that setup alongside OpenMW, so the modern engine is already sorted. Those mainland journeys start after a boat ride from the Vvardenfell you know. The team takes no donations and says the project will always stay free.

Stronghold Europe asks a simple question: what if Crusader's skirmish game had taken place in the green country of the first Stronghold? Community modders have worked on the idea since 2009, and the result swaps the deserts of the Holy Land for forests, fields and the cooler European look that many players still associate with the series.

It is a conversion rather than a texture pack. The landscapes change entirely, with birch trees and wolves among the scenery, and the interface and music are reworked to match the medieval mood of the original game. Everything that made Crusader's skirmish mode so replayable stays in place, so the AI lords, the economy and the siege warfare still work the way you expect them to, only on different ground.

That makes it a good pick for someone who loves Crusader's sandbox but misses the look of the 2001 game. It is less suited to anybody who wants a fresh story, because the appeal here is in skirmish and castle building. It also installs without overwriting the base game, and PlayBound keeps it apart from the clean HD and UCP3 editions, so you can move between them freely.

OpenLara's web edition is the quickest way to find out whether you still remember how to play 1996 Tomb Raider. There is nothing to install. It is XProger's open-source reimplementation of the classic engine running straight in the browser, with a demo level ready to go, so Lara's tank controls and square jumps are one click away.

It is not simply an old game in a window, either. The engine goes beyond a faithful copy, with better lighting, self-shadowing on Lara and enemies, and rewritten water effects that make those flooded rooms look far better than they did on period hardware. Frame rates are also no longer tied to the original's, so movement is much smoother than you may remember.

The limits follow from how it is delivered. This build is about the demo content, and the full games stay copyrighted: to play them through you need your own data and a standalone OpenLara build, which is what the desktop edition is for. That makes the web version best as a fast nostalgia check or something to show a friend who has never seen where Lara began. The project is open source under the BSD 2-Clause license.

expected.longDescription: OpenLara is a native engine for the original Tomb Raider games with OpenGL rendering, VR support, high frame rates and local co-op.

set.longDescription:
This is the fuller way to play OpenLara: XProger's open-source engine for classic Tomb Raider, as a standalone program rather than a browser tab. The engine's long-term goal is to run the original-era games from the first through the fifth, and the first Tomb Raider is the one its documentation describes as fully playable, so that is the best place to start.

Native builds are where its improvements have the most room. Frame rates are independent of the original's limits, with options as high as 144 frames per second, and resolution goes far beyond what 1996 allowed. Lighting is improved, with coloured light and self-shadowing, and the water is rewritten. There is even a first-person mode with Lara's hands in view, which changes how those long drops feel. This edition also adds headset support through OpenXR and two-player local split screen, two things no one expected from a 1996 tomb crawl.

OpenLara ships none of the original game's copyrighted files, so you bring your own Tomb Raider data. Expect some rough edges too, since this is a volunteer project still in progress. It is open source under the BSD 2-Clause license.

expected.longDescription: The official OpenRA Windows build. OpenRA recreates the classic Westwood RTS games - Red Alert, Tiberian Dawn and Dune 2000 - on a modern engine with online play, replays and map tools.

set.longDescription:
OpenRA is how Westwood's classic strategy games stay alive online. It is a free, open-source engine that rebuilds Command & Conquer: Tiberian Dawn, Red Alert and Dune 2000 for modern systems, and it is a good deal more than a compatibility patch: the games run natively, with a modern interface and a lively multiplayer scene that the originals lost long ago.

The improvements reach into how the games play. Online matches are built in, and the engine layers modern real-time strategy conveniences over the old designs. Each of the three mods keeps its own factions and feel, so the difference between GDI's slow armour and Nod's stealth, or between Allied navies and Soviet tanks, stays intact. The March 2025 release brought a heavily reworked map editor, better HD art for Tiberian Dawn, higher-quality Dune 2000 assets and more Red Alert missions.

It also doubles as a platform. Modders have used it to make whole new games, several of which PlayBound lists as their own editions, including Combined Arms. There is a stable release for online play and a playtest build for people who want to help test what comes next. Everything is free under the GPL version 3.

expected.longDescription: Combined Arms merges Tiberium, Red Alert, Dune and later C&C factions into one competitive OpenRA client. It ships as its own Windows portable build.

set.longDescription:
Combined Arms is a very simple idea executed at huge scale: take the best factions in Command & Conquer's history and let them fight in one game. Built on OpenRA, it puts the Allies, Soviets, GDI, Nod and the alien Scrin on the same battlefield, drawing units and technology from Tiberian Dawn, Red Alert and Tiberium Wars. PC Gamer's description of a giant five-faction brawl is about right.

It would be easy for that to fall apart, but this is a designed game rather than a pile of parts. The older Tiberian Dawn sides gain the tech centres, support powers and navies they never had. Each faction also splits into several sub-factions with their own units, super-weapons and support powers, so picking GDI is only the first decision of a match.

You can play skirmishes and multiplayer matches, or try singleplayer and co-operative missions, and the mod has kept growing since its 1.0 release in December 2023, with a major overhaul in August 2024 and further updates since. Best of all for newcomers, it is free and completely standalone: you need neither an original Command & Conquer game nor anything else installed. It runs on Windows, Linux and macOS.

expected.longDescription: Luanti, formerly Minetest, is a free, open-source voxel game engine. On its own it is a platform: games and mods are installed from the in-game content browser, and it supports multiplayer servers. This edition installs the official Windows build.

set.longDescription:
Luanti, known until 2024 as Minetest, is a free and open-source voxel engine, and that word matters: it is not one game but the thing that runs many. Install it and you get a block world platform plus access to a large library of games and mods, ranging from Minecraft-style survival to puzzles and experiments that have nothing much to do with digging.

The engine earns its reputation by being light and easy to change. Games and mods are written in Lua, so community projects appear constantly, and multiplayer servers send whatever mods they use to your client automatically, which means you can join a heavily modded world without preparing anything beforehand. Recent versions have brought an improved minimap, better particles and interface work, as well as a sizeable performance boost in version 5.15.

That makes it suit two kinds of player especially well: anyone on older hardware who wants a block game that runs well, and anyone who wants to tinker or build a game of their own. Just know what you are getting at the start: a fresh install is a launcher for content, so your first step is choosing a game. PlayBound lists several of the good ones here as editions.

expected.longDescription: Mineclonia is a performance-focused survival game for Luanti with mining, farming, enchanting and improved mob AI, built as a fork in the MineClone lineage.

set.longDescription:
Mineclonia is what to install on Luanti when you want the survival game you already know how to play. It is an unofficial, community-made Minecraft-like game that began in May 2023 as a fork of what is now VoxeLibre, and it set out with a tighter focus: stability, multiplayer performance, and following Minecraft's behaviour closely.

That focus shows in the details. Development pays special attention to accurate redstone and mob AI, the things that make a copy feel wrong when they are off. The Overworld runs 128 nodes deep, matching Minecraft 1.18 and later where VoxeLibre stops at 64. A few things go beyond the original as well, with bookshelves that actually hold books, Nether portals in custom shapes, a built-in crafting guide and an in-game help system, which saves a lot of trips to a wiki.

It also runs lighter than Java Edition, largely thanks to the Luanti engine underneath, so it suits older machines and friends' servers. It is fully moddable through Luanti's Lua API too. The honest caveat is that it is still in beta: it plays well, but it is not feature-complete, and an update can break an existing world, so keep backups of anything you care about.

expected.longDescription: A traditional roguelike dungeon crawler with randomised levels, dozens of enemies and hundreds of items, built on the open-source Pixel Dungeon by Watabou.

set.longDescription:
Shattered Pixel Dungeon is the roguelike many people mean when they say Pixel Dungeon now. It began in 2014 as a project to rebalance Watabou's original and has spent more than a decade growing past it, adding heroes, talents and systems while keeping the same simple premise: go down, get stronger, and accept that you will probably die on the way.

Every run has randomised levels, enemies and items, and there are hundreds of items to learn. Six hero classes play very differently: Warrior, Mage, Rogue, Huntress, Duelist and Cleric. Talents and subclasses then push each one further in the direction you choose, so a Mage on one run can have little in common with a Mage on the next. The depth comes from knowledge rather than twitch reflexes, because it is turn-based, and working out what an unidentified potion might do is part of the fun.

It is also unusually generous. The game is completely free on Windows, macOS, Linux and Android, with no adverts, microtransactions or paywalls, and its source is open under the GPL version 3. It is short enough for a lunch break per attempt, and hard enough that a first win can take a very long time.

expected.longDescription: Rat King Pixel Dungeon 2 rebuilds Shattered's Rat King April Fools mod as a full game. Heroes are dramatically buffed and the run is balanced around power.

set.longDescription:
RKPD2 is Shattered Pixel Dungeon with the sense of balance deliberately removed. It is a mod by Zrp200, first released in July 2021, that builds on Shattered and turns its playable Rat King into a ridiculous power trip. The developer's own release notes joked about how far the balance changes went, and that sense of humour is a fair guide to what you are in for.

The Rat King is the star. Rather than a normal hero with one path, he gets absurdly strong abilities, and the mod piles on further buffs to subclasses, armour abilities and tier 4 talents, including a big set of improvements to Ratmogrify. Quality-of-life changes and smaller levels mean that runs also move along more quickly than in the base game.

So it is not the place to learn Shattered, and it is not trying to be a fair challenge by default. It is what you play once you know the game and want to feel unreasonably strong for a while. There is still a test waiting for those who want one: the developer suggests a win with all nine challenges switched on as the true measure. Note that it is a different project from Rat King Adventure, which is listed separately.
